newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Wall St record pushes European shares higher.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Wall St record pushes European shares higher.

text.p: European shares made a strong start on Friday inspired by another record close on Wall Street, which rose on weak economic data that eased concerns about rising interest rates.
London shares were up 0.5 percent, while French and German shares were up 1.2 and 0.9 percent respectively by midmorning. All three made new trading records on the way up.
"This is Nirvana," Phil Orlando, U.S. based chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management, said of Wall Street's rise.
The Dow Jones industrial average surged 135.64 points to 7,711.47, its fifth record in a row. The index closed above 7,500 for the first time only on Tuesday, and ended at 7,575.83 on Wednesday.
"We'll take our cue now from Wall Street -- at least until this afternoon," one Frankfurt share trader said.

U.S. analysts said the American data, which included a surprising decline in U.S. retail sales over the last three months and a higher-than-expected level of weekly jobless claims, proved the country's economic growth remains within the Federal Reserve's -- and therefore the market's -- comfort zone.
Share traders on both sides of the Atlantic concluded there was less danger that interest rates would rise to choke off inflation -- good news for the share prices.
In London, the FTSE 100 advanced further into record ground and was up 24 points at 4,781.4 at 1000 gmt.
"If inflation is not picking up, these markets can be re-rated further," one London share trader said. "It's all liquidity driven."
German shares also surged to a record high of 3,751.26, helped by the dollar as well as Wall Street, though they then fell back a touch and stood at 3,742.84, up 34.85, at 0930 gmt.

Other factors pushing the market higher were abating fears about the future of European monetary union as France and Germany appeared ready to reach a compromise on a stability pact to ensure fiscal discipline after the start of the new currency in January 1999.

"There is more and more confidence out there that the euro will come on time, even if it's weaker than expected, so people now expect that money will keep coming into Europe after currency union," a trader said.

In Paris, the blue chip CAC share index rose to an all time high of 2,805.37 points, propelled by Wall Street and hopes of a ratification of a European stability pact at next week's EU Amsterdam summit, traders said. The CAC-40 index was up 34.08 points at 2,794.35 at 1000 GMT.
"There's a lot of volume out there," a broker said. He added that the message from the markets was that "in France, politics don't matter".

In currencies, the dollar steadied after a week of gyrations, with traders expecting it to tread water before next week's European Union summit and a meeting of leaders from the Group of Seven leading industrial nations.

Expectations that EU countries will adopt a stability pact which promotes fiscal discipline after the launch of the European single currency has boosted the dollar as much as three pfennigs from the week's lows against the mark.
Dollar/yen, meantime, is looking to the G7 meeting for reassurance the U.S. is not about to start a war of words over a recent rebound in Japan's trade and current account surpluses.
The dollar was quoted at 1.7290 marks at 1000 GMT and at 114.50 yen.

Hopes the G7 won't turn into a forum to criticise Japan's widening trade surpluses grew after U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said Thursday G7 leaders won't pay any special attention to U.S.-Japan trade flows, though the economic situation of both countries will be discussed.

Also, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said America will not use the dollar as an excessive instrument of trade policy. Still, he added that a sustained rise in Japan's trade surplus could hurt global growth and lead to a "protectionist backlash."

Dollar/mark was also broadly steady. Talk of a possible delay to European economic and monetary union, which triggered mark gains earlier this week, subsided as EU officials said they expected an accord on a deficit stability pact which requires countries to maintain fiscal discipline after joining EMU.
France had triggered the talk of delay after it asked Monday for time to consider the pact.
German and French leaders meeting in Poitiers, France today are expected by traders to reiterate their commitment to launching EMU in 1999 and their intention of adopting the stability pact.
CURRENCIES AT 1000 GMT
The dollar was at 1.7290 marks and 114.50 yen compared with 1.7265 marks and 113.99 yen in late European trade on Thursday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1000 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index finished was up 24 points at 4,781.4.
PARIS - The CAC-40 closed was up 34.08 points at 2,794.35.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was up 34.85 points at 3,742.84.
PRECIOUS METALS AT 1000 GMT
Gold was fixed at $341.20 in early European trade compared with $342.65 an ounce in late trade on Thursday.
